scenes.name: US Festival 1983 y el renacimiento del heavy
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: A principios de los ochenta la prensa rock habla de «revival» o «renacimiento» del heavy (Creem, octubre de 1980: el género «había hecho un Jesucristo»): nacen bandas en todo el mundo, las veteranas tocan para públicos mucho mayores y los medios se abren al metal. La señal más pública es el US Festival de 1983, patrocinado por Steve Wozniak: el día dedicado al heavy, con Ozzy, Judas Priest, Mötley Crüe, Scorpions, Quiet Riot, Van Halen y Triumph, reunió mucho más público que los otros dos.
scenes.family: Cultura metal: público, medios y conciertos

scenes.name: MTV y Headbangers Ball
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: MTV nace en agosto de 1981 y en dos años casi monopoliza el videoclip. El heavy, visual desde que Judas Priest se vistió de cuero, es un candidato natural: entre los primeros grupos emitidos están Quiet Riot, Mötley Crüe, Twisted Sister, Dokken y Scorpions, y la cuota de mercado del metal salta del 8 % en 1983 al 20 % en 1984 («MTV fue responsable del resurgir del heavy», dice Dee Snider). A principios de 1985 la presión fundamentalista lo recorta, pero en 1988 nace el programa nocturno «Headbangers Ball». MTV selecciona del metal lo compatible con un público juvenil general: hace del lite metal un coautor del género (pelo cardado, chico malo mono, chicas en el público) y empuja al thrash, casi ausente, a definirse como antítesis comercial. Los vídeos, rodados por directores de publicidad, cuestan cada vez más (190.000 dólares uno de Poison en 1989) y dejan fuera a las bandas pequeñas, convierten los conciertos en simulacros del vídeo y, al llevar el metal al salón familiar, despiertan a sus enemigos: la lista de los «Filthy Fifteen» del PMRC y el departamento de normas de MTV.

podcast.title: Early Formation and Industry Frustration
podcast.body: Quiet Riot formed eight years before 1984, playing in Los Angeles clubs like the Whisky a Go Go since the mid-1970s. The band members expressed significant frustration that fellow LA hard rockers Van Halen secured a major record deal before them, despite believing Quiet Riot was more popular. This perceived injustice contributed to Randy Rhoads' decision to leave the band and join Ozzy Osbourne. "The guys in quiet riot were pissed that their fellow LA hard rockers man hailing had been signed to a major record deal before they were."

podcast.title: MTV's Role in Early Band Exposure
podcast.body: Bassist Randy Sarzo explained that in MTV's early days, the channel lacked sufficient video content from bands, as music videos were not typically part of band budgets focused on radio airplay for publishing residuals. Record companies initially hesitated to fund expensive videos due to a perceived lack of return, but eventually saw increased record sales, which included publishing and mechanicals, as justification. Quiet Riot's first video for "Metal Health" cost $10,000, and the subsequent video for "Cum On Feel the Noize" cost $40,000, significantly boosting their exposure through constant rotation on MTV, even before MTV had widespread subscriptions, as stores and bars began playing the channel. "All of a sudden an MTV did not have enough content that is enough video from anybody. Those bands were not you was it wasn't part of the budget."

podcast.title: Post-Signing Industry Boom
podcast.body: After Quiet Riot finally secured their major record deal, Kevin Dubrow observed a sudden surge in similar signings across Los Angeles. He commented in 1984 that "now that we have signed they are signing every dimwit heavy metal band in LA," highlighting a shift in record company interest following their breakthrough. "Dubrow said in 1984 the funny thing is now that we have signed they are signing every dimwit heavy metal band in LA."

podcast.title: Randy Rhoads' Departure and Tragic Death
podcast.body: Randy Rhoads, an original member, left Quiet Riot to play with Ozzy Osbourne, partly due to the band's struggle to secure a major record deal before Van Halen. This period was also marked by various "shenanigans involving guns and intoxicating substances." Sadly, Rhoads died in a plane crash while on tour in 1982, a significant loss to the heavy metal community. "Rhodes left to go play with Aussie also there were. Various shenanigans involving guns and intoxicating substances sadly Rhodes died in a plane crash while on tour in 1982."
